articles.title: New WRU chairman Lyndon Faulkner to review plan to cut Welsh region
articles.summary: Lyndon Faulkner is not in his role yet but is already intent on getting to grips with both the WRU's finances and plans to cut a region.
articles.body:
New Welsh Rugby Union chair Lyndon Faulkner has confirmed he will review the controversial plan to cut a professional club in Wales.

The millionaire business magnate and former rugby player does not officially start his role until next month.

But he has already drawn up a list of priorities to get to grips with, including a review of the future number of regions and the union's "worrying" financial performance.

Faulkner - the nephew of Wales great Tony 'Charlie' Faulkner - hit back at suggestions he has been appointed to simply wave through the highly contested shake-up of professional rugby which will reduce the number of regions from four to three in 2028.

"There's talk out there that whoever took this job was under the condition that they can't talk about that [regional shake-up] but that's absolutely incorrect," said Faulkner.

"I wouldn't have taken the job with those conditions or if it were me needing to be a yes man. That's not me."

In his first interview since accepting the role, Faulkner admitted he was not aware of the full extent of the WRU's debt until it was announced last week.

"I feel it's my role to review everything we've got going on, challenge it, probe it and hopefully bring my experience to bear where I feel we can do things better.

"I haven't done what I've done in business by not doing that."

Asked if he would be prepared to row back on the WRU's decision to cut a region, Faulkner replied: "Absolutely - and that's on anything I see."

WRU bosses under pressure to resign after £18m loss

Scrum V: Is Welsh rugby living beyond its means?

WRU publishes data on why west Wales team will be cut

The 66-year-old is a fan of any potential Anglo-Welsh competition, having played in a similar competition for Pontypool in the 1980s, and broadly agreed with the WRU's decision to rescue Cardiff.

Faulkner will not be part of the WRU executive team, but he will chair the board and while he does not make the final decisions, he will wield major influence.

"They picked me because of my experience so it would be foolish to not take consideration of what I say," he said.

He is "empathetic" to the feelings of distrust from Ospreys and Scarlets - the two sides most at threat from closure - and was eager that a review would not prolong any decision over the regional shake-up which, he admitted, had already dragged on.

He said: "We've got four regions, all with their history in our great game. So I am understanding of the emotions that it drives. At the end of the day, we've got a review to do and then look at how that comes out."

Faulkner has plenty of experience of turning around the fortunes of struggling businesses.

The WRU may not be failing but, speaking at the Arms Park before a Super Rygbi Cymru match, Faulkner visibly grimaced when asked about the £18m loss posted for the latest financial year.

"That was quite a surprise to me because the previous finances didn't look that bad, but they are worrying," he said.

"So there is an absolute business aspect that has to be fixed and without that, we haven't got the right investments to go where we need the investments to go.

"There are no simple reasons, but there will be things we change or improve that will make a difference to those numbers, to manage costs and get revenue in.

"There's probably not a company in the UK at the moment, unless you're in oil and gas, that's not having some of the same issues with utility bills, minimum wages, national insurance or cost of food."

Coming from a famous rugby family, Faulkner made a name for himself after a knee injury ended his playing career, working for and eventually owning Welsh technology company Nimbus.

He talked Richard Branson into investing in CDs and then succeeded Robert Maxwell as owner of the business he later floated on the New York stock exchange.

He helped launch the Xbox and Microsoft Office before making his fortune trading and investing with some of the biggest tech companies in the United States - and even featured on Apprentice-style TV show The Mentor.

"$100m doesn't frighten me," he quipped.

But while Faulkner joked that not only his wife, but also close friends questioned his decision to get involved in the chaos of Welsh rugby, there was a heartfelt belief he can help provide solutions.

And he admitted he was frustrated by the "noise" generated by those voicing opinions "from the side of the ring" but unwilling to roll up their sleeves.

Swansea council leader Rob Stewart, ex-player Alex Cuthbert and businesswoman Hayley Parsons all called on WRU bosses to resign after the reported financial loss last week.

"Let's be honest, I'm putting my impeccable professional reputation on the line here," admitted Faulkner.

"But I'm actually getting in the ring. It frustrates me there's a lot of voices out there telling everybody what to do, but many of those voices are not prepared to actually get in the fight - and that list is quite extensive.

"It's also pretty distracting from the playing side. There are positive things happening, but we need people to support."

He added: "I don't need a job. I love Welsh rugby and this is purely motivated around trying to make a difference. I can apply all the things I've done in business but as an ex-player, I also understand rugby.

"There's no shortage of people telling me what we should be doing, but I think everybody in Wales wants us to do well, on and off the field. That's my goal."

Criticisms of his predecessor Richard Collier-Keywood were that he neither lived in Wales nor had any grounding in Welsh rugby. The merits of those arguments can be debated, but cannot apply to Faulkner.

As a centre, he played in the fearsome Pontypool team of the 1980s that was among the best in the UK and included the likes of Graham Price, Eddie Butler and David Bishop.

He won the Welsh Cup, represented Monmouthshire and twice faced Australia.

And while Wales honours eluded him behind the likes of Mark Ring and Dai Richards, Faulkner was shaped by working under inspirational coach Ray Prosser.

"He was an amazing man and there's a whole mix of emotions and things you learn under coaches like that," he recalled.

"I've always believed in the skills rugby teaches you, not just on the field but teamwork, camaraderie, competition, winning.

"And frankly, my success in business was taking many of those things to a business environment, building a team, having everybody look after each other's back and being tough."

While his uncle 'Charlie' Faulkner was a mainstay of a legendary Wales team of the past, Lyndon - whose son is finding his feet as a flanker in the Cardiff pathway - clearly believes he can be part of galvanising Welsh rugby's future.

articles.title: Prem talking points: Leicester vs Northampton fallout, Gloucester real deal & Christian Wade equals record
articles.summary: The main talking points from this weekend's Prem action, which was something of a throwback compared to the free-flowing rugby so far this season.
articles.body:
For all the free-flowing, high-scoring rugby in the Prem so far this season, this weekend was something of a throwback.

There were only 21 tries across the five games, whereas a fortnight ago there were 18 tries in the Northampton against Bath game alone.

But, despite the abominable weather altering the whole complexion of round four, there was no shortage of drama.

In the East Midlands derby on Saturday, Leicester Tigers produced a second-half performance that was as vintage Leicester Tigers as you could possibly get: a brutal set-piece and forward display that shook the old foundations of the Crumbie Stand and would have made the ABC Club proud.

In front of a febrile sell-out crowd, the game was played on the edge - a major scuffle breaking out on the stroke of half-time with England team-mates Henry Pollock and Ollie Chessum in the thick of it.

But tensions will have eased quickly. Thirteen of those involved in the derby met up for dinner in the England camp on Sunday.

"This fixture always has some heat behind it, and we know it means a lot to each other and to the fans," Leicester and England scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet explained to BBC Radio 5 Live.

"We just try and put all our heart on to the pitch. Sometimes it boils over into a little scuffle, but we will go and have a beer with them now. That's what rugby is about. You play fierce with each other and then enjoy each other's company.

"We always end up laughing about it. Being in England camp with them almost makes the fixture mean a bit more, because you always want one over them."

Northampton are the champions and still the team to beat. However, that's twice in six months they've been handed a lesson by the Tigers at Mattioli Woods Welford Road.

Saints fans will be comforted by the fact the title is decided in the warm early summer months of May and June, but boss Phil Dowson will still want his side to be as effective in the wet as they are in the dry.

England’s World Cup thinking and the rotation gamble

Are Gloucester now officially the real deal?

While the opening-round win at Exeter, the humiliation of Harlequins and the Champions Cup draw with the mighty Bordeaux were all impressive, the Friday night vanquishing of bitter rivals Bath was even better from the Cherry and Whites.

Tough up front and lively out wide, Gloucester have been a pleasure to watch this campaign, with centre Will Joseph rewarded with an England recall and the Wales talisman Jac Morgan the signing of the season so far.

It was as good a win, performance and atmosphere as Gloucester have had at Kingsholm in years.

"If you don't believe after these two weeks how good we could be then I don't know what you can do to get any more belief," said Glos boss George Skivington.

With Gloucester's defence inspired in the face of a Bath first-half onslaught, it was a great example of how a game of rugby doesn't need a bucketload of tries to be a captivating contest.

Speaking of tries, Christian Wade nabbed one more in Newcastle Red Bulls' victory over Sale, drawing him level with Chris Ashton's all-time record of 101 Prem scores.

It has been some journey for Wade to get to this point, with the popular 35-year-old playing for five different teams across three different sports since leaving Wasps at the peak of his powers in 2018.

Meanwhile, things are moving in the right direction for the Red Bulls. Last season Newcastle had to wait until round nine and the new year for the first of their two victories, this time they are up and running by the end of October.

A few weeks back Harlequins looked to be in crisis after a chastening 48-0 defeat at Gloucester. Since that low point, Quins have pushed Sale close, easily beaten French side Vannes and dispatched London rivals Saracens, with Marcus Smith to the fore on his 200th appearance.

Sale on the other hand, have followed up an impressive win at Sarries with a series of poor performances. Next the Sharks go to Bath, who themselves are stuttering after three defeats in a row.

What to make of it all? Just four rounds in, and it's already hard to keep up.

Gloucester are top and Harlequins are bottom. But Gloucester beat Bath, who beat Exeter, who beat Newcastle, who beat Sale, who beat Sarries, who beat Leicester, who beat Northampton, who beat Bath but lost to Bristol, who lost to Sarries, who lost to Quins.

It looks like it will be one of those seasons.

articles.title: Scotland: Newcastle's Ollie Leatherbarrow given first call-up
articles.summary: Uncapped Newcastle back row Ollie Leatherbarrow is called up by Scotland for the first time for the Nations Championship fixtures against New Zealand, Australia and Japan.
articles.body:
Uncapped Newcastle Red Bulls back row Ollie Leatherbarrow has been called up by Scotland for the first time for the three home Nations Championship fixtures against New Zealand, Australia and Japan.

But in-form Edinburgh forwards Magnus Bradbury and Freddy Douglas are surprising omissions from the 37-strong squad.

Macclesfield-born Leatherbarrow qualifies for Scotland because of his grandmother being from Perth and has already represented Scotland at under-16 and under-20 levels.

The 24-year-old began his career at Exeter Chiefs before moving to Newcastle in 2023. Senior trio Jamie Ritchie, Darcy Graham and Duhan van der Merwe have all been included after returning recently from injuries.

"This has been my goal for a long time," said Leatherbarrow. "When you feel like you are playing well for your club, your obviously looking to get that national call-up.

"It's just about showing what I can do. My strength is probably ball-carrying, so that lends itself to number eight a bit more, but I'm probably more the size of a seven.

"I've played all three back row positions for Newcastle and I'm happy to play wherever really."

Head coach Gregor Townsend acknowledged Bradbury's strong start to the season but said he was "looking for more" from the 31-year-old.

"We know Magnus is hugely motivated for Scotland," he explained. "We know the qualities he brings. We're also aware that Jack Dempsey [now based in Japan] is not going to be available in the Six Nations, so it's an opportunity for us to look at someone else in our environment.

"We know Ollie can cover all three positions in the back row. He's an openside by trade, but he's played a lot of rugby at six and eight. He'll be challenging for a place now and in the Six Nations, like Magnus will be as well."

Glasgow Warriors' Seb Stephen, who made his debut in July's Nations Championship match against Fiji, is one of three hookers selected.

Experienced Edinburgh lock Grant Gilchrist is not included after returning from injury, while club-mate Hector Patterson had been touted for potential involvement after a bright start to the season, but the scrum-half has not made the cut.

Townsend said no decision has been made yet on New Zealand-born Josh McKay, the 29-year-old Glasgow full-back who will be eligible in time for the final Test against Japan.

Scotland host the All Blacks on 7 November, the Wallabies on 15 November and the Brave Blossoms on 21 November at Murrayfield before the new Nations Championship concludes the following weekend at Twickenham, based around final hemisphere positions.

The finals are on the weekend of 28-29 November, with fixtures determined by the placings of northern and southern hemisphere countries across these games and the ones played in July.

Forwards: Ewan Ashman (Edinburgh), Josh Bayliss (Bath), Gregor Brown, Scott Cummings, Alex Craig, Rory Darge (all Glasgow Warriors), Jack Dempsey (Toshiba Brave Lupus), Matt Fagerson, Zander Fagerson (both Glasgow Warriors), Jonny Gray (Perpignan), Gregor Hiddleston (Glasgow Warriors), Will Hurd (Leicester Tigers), Ollie Leatherbarrow (Newcastle Red Bulls), Nathan McBeth (Glasgow Warriors), Liam McConnell (Edinburgh), Elliot Millar Mills (Newcastle Red Bulls), Jamie Ritchie (Glasgow Warriors), Pierre Schoeman (Edinburgh), Rory Sutherland, Seb Stephen, Max Williamson (all Glasgow Warriors).

Backs: Fergus Burke (Saracens), Jamie Dobie (Glasgow Warriors), Darcy Graham (Edinburgh), George Horne (Glasgow Warriors), Rory Hutchinson (Northampton Saints), Huw Jones (Toulon), Tom Jordan (Bristol Bears), Blair Kinghorn (Toulouse), Stafford McDowall, Kyle Rowe (both Glasgow Warriors), Finn Russell (Bath), Ollie Smith, Kyle Steyn, Sione Tuipulotu, capt (all Glasgow Warriors), Duhan van der Merwe (Edinburgh), Ben White (Toulon).

articles.title: Steve Borthwick and England's selection dilemmas amid World Cup countdown
articles.summary: The upcoming Nations Championship matches present a selection dilemma for Steve Borthwick's England with just nine matches to go until the World Cup.
articles.body:
With under a year to go until the 2027 Rugby World Cup, the countdown is on, with just nine competitive matches for the home nations until the tournament starts in Australia next October.

But while the World Cup spectre looms large, there is plenty to play for between now and then, starting with the resumption of the inaugural Nations Championship in November.

Steve Borthwick has named his 36-man training squad ahead of the Tests with Australia, Japan and New Zealand, and it gives a clear indication of the England head coach's thinking on both a long and short-term basis.

England play Australia on 8 November before facing Japan on 14 November and New Zealand on 21 November.

There is a recall for Joe Marchant, fellow centre Will Joseph is rewarded for his and Gloucester's excellent start to the season, while uncapped Archie McParland is the third scrum-half and uncapped Kepu Tuipulotu the third hooker.

On the whole, though, it is a tried and tested group.

"If we look at this training squad, it's not picked on form, is it?" former England wing Chris Ashton said on the Rugby Union Weekly podcast.

"It is a squad to get to the World Cup. Will Joseph is picked on form, but the vast majority is not. It is based on the experience and relationships [Borthwick] has with the players, and that is why Marchant is in there."

It is often the dilemma facing an England head coach. With 10 teams to pick from, there are always players playing well. How do you balance that with getting selection consistency from campaign to campaign?

Fin Baxter, Luke Cowan-Dickie, Jamie George, Will Stuart, George Furbank and Ben Curry - among others - have all been short of minutes or form this season. But they are all Borthwick regulars with priceless Test match experience.

"Part of the problem right now is that Steve feels he is under pressure to get results, so it is too late to make big changes," added Ashton.

"There just aren't many lads that have played much rugby."

Injury absences and a midfield conundrum

The uncapped pair of McParland and Tuipulotu will both bring a freshness to camp.

But will McParland get much gametime ahead of the established duo of Jack van Poortvliet and Alex Mitchell, and will Tuipulotu get any minutes when competing with the highly experienced George and Cowan-Dickie?

"We know how talented Tuipulotu is, he is brilliant, but Nathan Jibulu at Sale has had two man-of-the-match performances and might feel slightly hard done by," said Ugo Monye, who also added that George Hendy at Northampton is another notable omission.

"In my opinion, we need to have a look at Hendy," he continued.

"He has been that good for that long. And if we are talking about form, where is [Bristol back rower] Fitz Harding?

"But I am sure Steve had a rough idea of his squad a month ago."

As ever, injuries will force Borthwick's hand.

Benhard Janse van Rensburg is out - a big blow to Borthwick given how he was fast-tracked into the set-up - while incumbent number 12 Seb Atkinson is on the rehab list, as is Exeter flyer Immanuel Feyi-Waboso. Their fitness will be monitored forensically by the England medical staff.

Meanwhile, the nailed-on starter at fly-half Fin Smith will also miss training this week with a calf niggle, although his injury is not thought to be serious. Charlie Atkinson was called up on Monday morning.

In the forwards, the selection picture is reasonably clear. Ellis Genge, George, Cowan-Dickie, Joe Heyes, Will Stuart, Ollie Chessum, Alex Coles, Maro Itoje, George Martin, Ben Earl, Tom Curry and Henry Pollock all make the 23 if fit.

Behind the scrum, especially at centre, it is more uncertain.

"I would struggle to answer [who will play in the midfield]," said Ashton.

Atkinson and Henry Slade started England's last Test, a crucial victory over Argentina in July, and could line up together again against the Wallabies on 8 November.

But Marchant and Joseph are also battling for the number 13 shirt, and a possible World Cup place.

"Marchant and Will Joseph are in a bit of a shoot-out," added Monye.

"They can both do a job on the wing and when you look at a World Cup squad you look at versatility.

"I would like to see bold decisions, but it is easy saying that when your job isn't on the line and you are trying to get selection right ahead of a World Cup.

"Will Joseph has been excellent and there will loads of fans who watch the Prem and will say against Australia, Seb Atkinson and Will Joseph are your ready-made 12 and 13.

"But I would be very surprised if that was to happen."

The players will be in camp until Tuesday evening before returning to their clubs for one more round of league action, before re-joining England next Sunday, seven days before the Australia showdown.

Borthwick has precious little time in camp with his squad before the Wallabies come to town, putting even more emphasis on established players, and established combinations.

Twelve months ago, England were in the midst of a winning run and started the autumn series full of confidence.

It is a different picture now after an underwhelming 2026, with just three wins from eight matches so far. As it stands, where the side will be come the World Cup in 12 months is anyone's guess.

England and Borthwick need a big November.

articles.title: World Rugby Player of the Year: England's Zoe Harrison and Meg Jones among nominees
articles.summary: England pair Zoe Harrison and Meg Jones are named among the nominees for the World Rugby Player of the Year award.
articles.body:
England duo Zoe Harrison and Megan Jones are among four nominees for World Rugby Women's 15s Player of the Year award.

They are nominated alongside Canada's DaLeaka Menin and New Zealand's Kaipo Olsen-Baker for the award, which recognises exceptional performances during the 2026 season.

Fly-half Harrison, 28, scored 88 points from the tee for England this year while Red Roses captain Jones, 30, is nominated for a second year in a row - missing out to Canada's Sophie de Goede in 2025.

The World Cup-winning pair played important roles in England claiming their eighth successive Women's Six Nations title in May, part of a 41-match unbeaten run ended by back-to-back defeats by Canada this month.

The winner will be announced following this weekend's final WXV Global Series matches, with England facing the United States on Friday (21:15 GMT).

Elsewhere, England's Abi Burton has been shortlisted for Women's 15s Try of the Year for her try against Australia in the WXV Global Series in September.

articles.title: Tadhg Furlong: Ireland prop cited for alleged groin grab on Gavin Coombes
articles.summary: Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong is cited over an alleged groin grab in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster on Saturday.
articles.body:
Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong has been cited over an alleged groin grab in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster on Saturday.

Munster back row Gavin Coombes raised the allegation against an unnamed Leinster player with match referee Andrew Brace in the closing stages of the first half at the Aviva Stadium, but television match official (TMO) Colin Stanley could not find any video evidence at the time.

However, experienced front row Furlong has now been cited over an act of foul play under Law 9.27, which says a "a player must not do anything that is against the spirit of good sportsmanship including but not limited to grabbing, twisting or squeezing the genitals".

A statement from the URC said "arrangements for the disciplinary process are currently in progress and will be announced in due course".

If found guilty of the offence, the 33-year-old would be in danger of missing Ireland's Nations Championship matches with Argentina, Fiji and South Africa in Dublin, as well as the finals weekend in London.

In October 2025, South Africa front-rower Jan-Hendrik Wessels received a nine-match suspension for grabbing Josh Murphy's genitals in the Bulls' URC win over Connacht.

For that incident, Wessels was handed a 12-week suspension - the shortest ban under World Rugby rules for such an offence - that was reduced by three weeks due to his "good conduct prior to and at the hearing and good record".

If similar action was taken against Furlong, he would potentially miss Leinster's Investec Champions Cup Pool match with Sale, as well as the festive inter-provincial derbies with Ulster and Munster.

Speaking after the 24-18 defeat at the Aviva Stadium , Munster head coach Clayton McMillan said he would "back our players 100% that if they make an allegation like that".

Leinster head coach Leo Cullen said he did not see the incident, which occurred in the 37th minute when Munster were leading, but acknowledged it was a "serious matter".

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: Brian Carney warns England ‘have it all to do’ to avoid group-stage exit
articles.summary: England’s hopes of reaching the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals hang in the balance, with their progression dependent on other results; Brian McDermott's side must beat Papua New Guinea on Friday, with Tonga facing Samoa on Sunday
articles.body:
England's 30-12 defeat to Tonga in their opening match raised doubts over their chances of reaching the knockout stages.

Even after sealing an 82-0 victory against France on Saturday, Brian McDermott's side still need a series of events to go their way to qualify .

England must beat Papua New Guinea (PNG) in Wollongong on Friday by a large margin. They will then need to wait two days to learn their fate, with Tonga set to play Samoa in Sydney on Sunday.

A Samoa victory would send England out, while a Tonga win could see them progress on points difference.

"The whistle went on the Tonga game and everybody went: 'Well, this format is appalling. England are essentially out. It's one and done in the tournament'," Sky Sports Rugby League's Carney said.

"They went out against France and they built a huge scoreline to give themselves hope.

"They're going to have to do the same again against a PNG side who I have found disappointing in the tournament so far. They will need Tonga to beat Samoa so they're going to need an awful lot to go their way."

This year's tournament features a unique format, with six teams included in Pool B and C. If multiple teams finish tied, final group standings will be determined by teams' head-to-head record.

That means Tonga would finish above England in the standings after their first-round victory.

England trail Samoa by a points difference margin of 68 heading into the final round of fixtures and will need to cut that deficit with a big win against PNG to leapfrog Samoa.

"What England have to do, and you've heard this a thousand times in different sports, is control the controllables," Carney said.

"They'll have to go out, pile on the points, and the more points they put over, the less Tonga have to win by."

England Women must change to catch up with Australia

England women were outclassed by Australia on Saturday, suffering a 78-0 defeat to the defending world champions .

The defeat follows Stuart Barrow's side's 90-4 loss to the Jillaroos in Las Vegas in March 2025, raising further questions about the gap between England and the world's leading teams.

Despite opening the tournament with a commanding 70-6 victory over Wales, England must beat Samoa in a winner-takes-all final group-stage clash on Saturday to secure their place in the knockout stages.

Reflecting on the heavy defeat to Australia, McDermott acknowledged that significant changes are needed across all levels of rugby league in the UK if England are to close the gap on the Jillaroos.

"I'd ask this question: 'What did one expect?'" Carney said.

"The English women's side, it's coming from a competition that is struggling for competitive games, struggling for resources, against a Jillaroos side who are very well resourced, in a very competitive environment with very strong competition, and all the best players in the world are in Australia's competition - the NRLW.

"So I'm not sure what people expected the game to be. Was it an improvement on the Las Vegas defeat? Marginally on the scoreboard.

"Some will argue they have seen signs that England have turned the corner. I'm not so sure.

"Unless you sort out the competition over here, and rugby league in this part of the world, and everybody is adequately funded, you're not going to close the gap."

articles.title: Totoa Auvaa: Bristol sign Samoan forward sacked by Saracens
articles.summary: Bristol Bears have signed 21-year-old Samoan forward Totoa Auvaa, two weeks after he was sacked by Saracens.
articles.body:
Bristol Bears have signed Samoan forward Totoa Auvaa, two weeks after he was sacked by Saracens.

Auvaa, 21, was involved in a nightclub altercation with England cricketers Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson in June.

He was let go by Sarries following another incident in St Albans, which police are investigating.

"His agent reached out to me to see if I would be willing to help him and give him a second chance," Bristol's director of rugby Pat Lam said.

"I've always believed that young people deserve the opportunity to learn from those experiences, grow and become better people."

Lam, himself a former Samoan international, told Bristol's website , external he believed the club could help provide support to Auvaa and was the right place for him to develop on and off the field.

"Totoa is a big, physical young man with enormous potential, who unfortunately has made some mistakes since arriving from a small village in Samoa to the massive city of London.

"Having spent time with Totoa, I feel confident that we can provide him with the mentorship, guidance, support and structure to give him the best possible opportunity to succeed, not just as a rugby player, but as a person - someone his parents and family all the way back in Samoa will be proud of."

Two punch-ups, two red cards, no chances left - Saracens sack Auvaa

Saracens sack academy player Auvaa after latest incident

Auvaa's disciplinary issues have not been restricted to late-night altercations.

While on loan at Championship club Ampthill last season, he was sent off twice for violent conduct - once, punching an opposition player in the face in the aftermath of conceding a try, and, in another match, kicking someone in the head at the bottom of a ruck.

Auvaa's youth, recent arrival in England and the stress of supporting his father through illness back home in Samoa were put forward in mitigation.

When he was involved in the nightclub incident with Atkinson and Stokes, in which a member of England's security staff was left bloodied after being struck by Auvaa , Saracens said they would stand by him.

However, after the incident in St Albans, the club said , external his conduct had fallen "short of the standards expected of everyone who represents Saracens, both on and off the pitch" and he was sacked.

A statement issued by Hertfordshire Police on the incident said: "Police are investigating an altercation which occurred between 0215 and 0220 on Sunday [11 October] in St Peter's Street, St Albans.

"It is alleged a man aged in his twenties was approached by another man who then punched him to the face. Enquiries are ongoing at this time."

Auvaa made one appearance for Saracens, playing 20 minutes of a Prem Rugby Cup match in September.

articles.title: Ulster Rugby: Richie Murphy confident of URC turnaround after winless start
articles.summary: Head coach Richie Murphy says Ulster are "small margins" away from a first victory in the United Rugby Championship after a winless start in the league.
articles.body:
On the face of it, Ulster are without a victory in their four United Rugby Championship outings this season.

But head coach Richie Murphy is not ready to hit the panic button.

Despite a winless start, the Irish province are just one point outside the play-off places despite a struggle for results.

An opening defeat by Edinburgh was followed by two thrilling draws against Glasgow and Munster, and then a loss to the Bulls in the first of a South African double-header.

There has been a constant theme throughout: Ulster have allowed the opposition to build an early - and often significant - lead.

On each occasion they have fought back, but have yet to seal a comeback with victory.

Murphy admits his side have been "digging a bit of a hole" in each of their four matches this season.

"Obviously, we're not quite getting the results that we wanted, but we're in every game," said Murphy, whose side defeated Zebre in their Challenge Cup opener.

"We're playing against top-class opposition and we're fighting for everything we can get."

"It's really important that we don't throw the baby out with the bathwater. We will stick to our process and stick to what we believe in, and that's what we're trying to do."

McNabney keen to show Ireland coaches 'what I'm all about'

Murphy praises Ulster for 'sticking in the fight'

Despite admitting the opening results have left him with "mixed emotions", Murphy feels his side "can compete with the best teams in the league".

"We're not a million miles away from winning opportunities to win every one of those matches," he added.

"We're just trying to double down on the areas that we need to improve. If you ask me what areas are they, it's a little bit of everything.

"If we could be a little bit better at the breakdown, or if our pass quality could be a little bit better. All these tiny little aspects of the game add up to wins."

If Ulster are to pick up an elusive first URC victory of the season, Murphy knows that consistency is going to be key - starting against the Stormers in Cape Town on Saturday (12:45 GMT).

"In each of the games that we've played, we've played some very high-class rugby in both attack and defence, but we haven't been consistent," he said.

"The thing that we strive for is consistency and if our execution can very slightly improve, it's amazing what that will do to the results.

"We'll stick to the process, believe in what we're trying to do and we believe that the results will come."

While Ulster have been soaking up the heat in South Africa - a stark contrast to the current weather back home - Murphy knows his side are about to face a storm of a different kind on Saturday.

The Stormers will likely have their Springbok stars available - such as Siya Kolisi, back row Evan Roos and fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu - which is not a luxury Murphy will have.

In fact, Ulster head to Cape Town without nine of their key players after they were called up for Ireland duty ahead of November's Nations Championship fixtures.

Backs Stuart McCloskey, Jacob Stockdale, Robert Baloucoune, Nathan Doak and Jamie Benson have been included along with forwards Tom O'Toole, Tom Stewart, James McNabney and Nick Timoney.

The experience of hooker Rob Herring and centre James Hume should help to fill the void despite their lack of minutes through injury, and returning wing Zac Ward will offer plenty of try-scoring prowess.

Murphy admits it "causes a different headache for us" having so many players unavailable.

"We didn't know the amount of players we were going to lose and nine is probably more than we were expecting.

"But at the same time, we're delighted for those players to get the opportunity to go and represent Ireland."

Of the nine players called up for Ireland's Nations Championship games in November, Benson and McNabney have been called up for the first time.

Murphy said Benson, a versatile Irish-qualified former England Under-20 international, has been "excellent" since joining from Harlequins in the summer.

The 24-year-old has featured in both centre positions and fly-half for Ulster, and can also play at full-back.

"He has shown good signs of leadership in our group as well and his attitude has been so good in relation to playing in three different positions

"That versatility is really good for any squad and Ireland are obviously recognising that as well."

Back row McNabney, who Farrell described as "some specimen", has been included after recovering from a year on the sidelines with an ACL injury.

"He's finding his feet in a little bit, but you can see the attributes that he has," said Murphy.

"It's great to have those guys in there, but it obviously puts pressure on our squad."

articles.title: Where are Wales internationals really made? BBC Sport traced the last 100
articles.summary: Where a player is born in only one part of the story - BBC Sport traces the playing journey of Wales' 100 most recent internationals.
articles.body:
Born in Wales, educated in one region, polished in another and given a professional debut somewhere else. The journey to a Wales jersey is rarely as straightforward as the badge on a player's shirt.

Where does a Wales international come from?

For most, the answer is Wales. But that only tells a fraction of the story.

BBC Sport has traced the past 100 men to make their Wales debuts - from where they were born, through junior clubs and schools, into academies, first professional appearances and the clubs they represent today.

It is a journey that starts on local playing fields, crosses the Severn Bridge and sometimes stretches halfway around the world.

And with the future shape of Welsh professional rugby under scrutiny, it helps explain who does what in producing an international.

The research divides each player's journey into five stages. Some classifications require judgement where pathways overlap; our full approach is explained in the methodology at the end of this article.

Of the past 100 Wales debutants, 76 were born in Wales, 17 in England and seven elsewhere.

That overseas group includes New Zealand-born Hadleigh Parkes and Johnny McNicholl, as well as Bradley Roberts, who was born in South Africa. Their birth certificates tell you very little about where they became professional rugby players.

Equally, being born in Wales does not mean a player stayed there. Louis Rees-Zammit and Dafydd Jenkins are two examples of Welsh-born talent whose route to the senior game led them across the border.

The more revealing question is what happened after those players first picked up a rugby ball.

For 78 of the 100, their formative rugby education - up to age 16 - was in Wales.

We looked at schools, junior clubs and the areas in which players grew up playing, rather than attributing a child's development to whichever professional academy eventually signed him.

Cardiff's catchment accounts for 30 of the players, followed by the Ospreys area with 20, Scarlets with 17, Dragons with 10 and North Wales with one.

These are not 30 Cardiff academy graduates or 20 Ospreys academy graduates. They are players who learned their rugby in those geographical areas, often thanks to volunteers, teachers and local clubs.

Rees-Zammit is a useful illustration. His early rugby was in the Cardiff area, but his pathway would take him to Gloucester. Tommy Reffell developed in the Ospreys area before Leicester Tigers became the next stop on his journey.

For both, the Welsh rugby education came first. The professional breakthrough came elsewhere.

At 16, the journey changes. Rugby becomes more specialised, academies matter more and the question shifts from learning the game to preparing for professional rugby.

In our sample, 70 players followed their main late-teenage development pathway in Wales. Cardiff accounted for 26, Scarlets 18, Ospreys 15, Dragons nine, with one in north Wales and one through another Welsh route.

England accounted for 24. Among them were players who had started their rugby education in Wales but moved to English development systems.

Sam Costelow, for example, moved from the Ospreys pathway to Leicester. Reffell's route also took him to Welford Road while Jenkins developed at Exeter.

The traffic is not all one way. James Botham grew up in England before joining Cardiff's development system and making his professional breakthrough there.

The figures do not establish which academy is "best". They show how often the work of developing a Wales player is shared between different places — and sometimes different countries.

Who gave them their first professional chance?

Here the question is deliberately narrower: which fully professional club first selected each player for a senior appearance? An earlier game in the semi-professional Welsh Premiership does not count.

Seventy-four of the 100 made that first professional appearance with a Welsh region; 26 with Cardiff or Cardiff Blues, 19 with Scarlets, 19 with Ospreys and 10 with Dragons.

The remaining 26 began their fully professional careers outside the four Welsh regions.

The distinction between academy and debut matters. Ben Warren was developed in Cardiff's academy, but his first senior professional appearance came with the Ospreys in October 2022.

Rees-Zammit's first professional opportunity came at Gloucester, Reffell's at Leicester and Jenkins' at Exeter.

An academy can nurture a player without giving him his debut. A professional club can provide the opportunity without having taught him the game. Both roles matter.

Finally, we looked at where those 100 players were playing in October 2026 — or whether they had retired.

Sixty-one were with Welsh regions: Cardiff 19, Scarlets 15, Ospreys 15 and Dragons 12.

Another 28 were playing elsewhere, while 11 had finished their professional careers. Of the 89 still active, more than two-thirds were therefore employed by the four Welsh regions.

But this is a snapshot, not a permanent tally of players 'lost' to Welsh rugby. Careers move in both directions. Players leave, return, change regions and sometimes take opportunities abroad for reasons that have little to do with where they were developed.

Put the five stages together and the message is clear: there is no single factory producing Wales internationals.

Junior clubs and schools provide most of the foundations. Welsh academies and professional regions remain central. English and overseas clubs play a significant role too.

At a moment when the future structure of the Welsh game is being debated, those distinctions are worth understanding. A player's journey is rarely the work of just one club.

BBC Sport examined Wales men's international debutants numbered 1125 to 1224, using player biographies, club and competition records, school and junior-club histories, and Gareth Rhys Owen's own rugby commentary research notes accumulated while preparing for broadcasts. The working database was cross-referenced and individual pathway decisions were reviewed.

Birthplace is the recorded town and country of birth. Formative rugby education covers the main junior club, school and local rugby catchment up to approximately age 16.

Finishing development covers the main academy or equivalent pathway from roughly 16 to 20.

First professional club means the club of the player's first senior appearance in a fully professional competition; semi-professional Welsh Premiership appearances are excluded.

Current club or retirement status is a snapshot at 9 October 2026.

The four Welsh regional labels used for early education describe broad geographical rugby catchments, not necessarily formal academy membership. Some players moved between systems, so identifying one principal pathway involved editorial judgement.

This is a study of the past 100 Wales debutants, not all professional players or a controlled ranking of academy performance.

articles.title: England rugby league: Jez Litten and Morgan Knowles in, Brad O'Neill out for crucial World Cup match
articles.summary: Jez Litten and Morgan Knowles are brought into the starting line-up for England's must-win Rugby League World Cup match against Papua New Guinea - with Brad O'Neill dropping out.
articles.body:
Jez Litten and Morgan Knowles have been brought into the starting line-up for England's must-win Men's Rugby League World Cup match against Papua New Guinea - with Brad O'Neill dropping out of the squad.

Hull KR's Litten comes in at hooker as head coach Brian McDermott chases a big victory in their final Group B-C match in Wollongong on Friday (09:05 GMT) to keep alive hopes of reaching the semi-finals.

O'Neill, named the best player in Super League in 2026, is not in the 19-player matchday squad, having worn the number nine for last Saturday's victory over France.

Dolphins lock Knowles comes in after missing the opening two matches with a calf injury, replacing Victor Radley, who drops to the bench.

Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand

Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app

Warrington's Matty Ashton, brought in for the France match, retains his place on the wing, with Wigan's Zach Eckersley again not in the matchday 19.

McDermott, however, has made late changes to his initial matchday squad for both of England's two matches so far, and may do so again before Friday.

On the backfoot since being beaten 30-12 by Tonga in their opening game, England responded with a crushing 82-0 victory over France to keep alive their dreams.

England need to beat co-hosts PNG – then hope Tonga beat Samoa, two days later in Sydney.

If Samoa win, England will be eliminated because of their inferior head-to-head record against Tonga.

But if Tonga win, it comes down to points difference between England and Samoa - with England's currently 68 points worse than the Samoans.

The match is part of a triple header in Wollongong, with England's wheelchair team starting the defence of their World Cup title against Wales (04:30 GMT) before the women's side face Samoa (06:45 GMT).

Roche in for women's must-win Samoa match

Georgia Roche replaces Jenna Foubister at half-back for England women, with Hope Millard stepping up to the bench for their must-win final group game.

England have to beat Samoa to finish second in Group A and qualify for the semi-finals.

They beat Wales 70-6 in their opener, but were thrashed 78-0 by reigning champions Australia in Perth last weekend.

Foubister, 19, started against Australia after a superb domestic season where she was named Super League Woman of Steel.

But she struggled against the strength of Australia, so coach Stu Barrow has opted for the experience of Roche instead.

The loss of key player Eva Hunter to a leg injury suffered against the Jillaroos has prompted a pack reshuffle, with Hollie-Mae Dodd moving from prop to the back row.

Mary Coleman comes in at prop as a result, while England are boosted by captain Jodie Cunningham overcoming an ear injury suffered last week to be named on the bench.

Georgia Wilson is in for Molly Jones in the centres, while Millard - the only heritage player left in the England set-up following Jasmin Strange's tournament-ending knee injury - is back in the squad.

A win would earn England a semi-final spot, where they would most likely face New Zealand, who beat them in the last four of the previous World Cup in 2022.

Dual-code international Ffion Lewis returns to the Wales side for their final Group A match, against world champions Australia in Sydney on Sunday (04:40 GMT). Carys Marsh steps up from the bench and will start at hooker.

Australia - already assured of a semi-final place - have made several changes. Stand-off Jocelyn Kelleher, who was outstanding against England last Saturday, is rested with Jesse Southwell taking her place.

Walsh returns for Australia in final group game

Australia coach Kevin Walters has recalled Reece Walsh at full-back for their final Group A game against the Cook Islands on Saturday (09:05 GMT).

Walsh, whose 2026 domestic season was disrupted by injury troubles, started Australia's thrilling World Cup opener against New Zealand.

He scored a try but kicked just two of five conversions as the Kangaroos squeezed to a 24-22 win. He was then rested against Fiji in their second group match, which Australia won 36-22.

Walsh returns in place of James Tedesco at full-back, with Cameron Munster returning at stand-off as Sam Walker drops out of the 19, and Harry Grant regaining the number nine hooker's jersey.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: England draft Jez Litten and Morgan Knowles into starting line-up for crunch Papua New Guinea match
articles.summary: Brian McDermott has opted to bring Jez Litten and Morgan Knowles into his starting line-up for England's crunch Rugby League World Cup clash against Papua New Guinea on Friday; Brad O'Neill drops out of the matchday squad
articles.body:
Brad O'Neill drops out of the 19-player matchday squad after featuring in England's 82-0 victory against France on Saturday.

Brian McDermott's side must secure victory in their final Group B and C match to keep their hopes of reaching the semi-finals alive. They will then face a nervous two-day wait for Tonga's clash against Samoa.

If Samoa win, England will be knocked out of the Rugby League World Cup at the group stage for the first time in history due to their head-to-head record against Tonga.

Tonga are guaranteed to finish above England, having won two games, including their 30-12 win against McDermott's side in their tournament opener.

But England can advance on points difference if they beat Papua New Guinea by a large margin and Tonga secure a convincing victory against Samoa.

Litten will take over from O'Neill at hooker for his first start in the tournament, while Knowels will play as England's loose forward, after missing England's first two matches due to injury.

Victor Radley, who wore the No 13 jersey against France, has dropped to the bench.

Litten, who started as an interchange during England's match against France, came on to score in the 58th minute, while Herbie Farnworth, who scored a hat-trick of tries, keeps his place in the centres alongside Hugo Savala.

articles.title: United Rugby Championship: Ulster's Juarno Augustus relishing South Africa homecoming
articles.summary: Ulster back row Juarno Augustus is relishing being back in his native South Africa as he prepares to face his former club Stormers after recovering from ankle surgery.
articles.body:
Ulster back row Juarno Augustus says he is "enjoying his rugby again" after recovering from the ankle surgery he underwent in the summer.

This weekend the 28-year-old is preparing to go back to where it all began in terms of his professional playing career as the Irish province face the Stormers in a United Rugby Championship encounter.

Augustus, who played for the Cape Town-based side between 2017 and 2021, is relishing the prospect of coming up against his former team while also spending some precious time with his family.

"It's nice just to be at home. I'll probably need a lot of tickets, everyone's been asking me!" said the former Northampton Saints forward.

"It's always nice to play against the team you grew up playing for. I'll just try to play my game to the best of my ability.

"I had surgery and I was struggling a bit in pre-season to put it behind me but it's all gone now and I've had a run of games. That's the main thing - to keep training and being fit again. "

Four games, no wins - Ulster aim for URC turnaround

Ulster remain without a victory in their URC campaign to date, their 34-26 defeat by the Bulls in Pretoria extending their winless run in the competition this season to four games.

"I don't think huge things need to change. It's just a bounce of the ball, just small things that we need to work on and get right," added Augustus.

Ulster and the Stormers played out a pulsating 38-38 draw in Belfast last term but the number eight is hoping Richie Murphy's side can go one better on Saturday (12:45 GMT) against a Stormers outfit who have won three and lost one of their four URC matches.

"It's at their home this time so we need to be sharper, need to be ready for what they're going to bring. From minute one to minute 80, we need to give it our best. That's what we are going after.

"They have a lot of dangerous players who can make anything happen in a second. We need to be aware of it.

"Richie and his coaching staff gave us some detail on how they play and it's up to us now to go out and execute.

"We just need to be on our game every single moment."

articles.title: Scotland: Gregor Townsend has belief against New Zealand that lacked as a player
articles.summary: Head coach Gregor Townsend on the challenge of finding Scotland's first win over New Zealand and getting high-ball help from Australia.
articles.body:
On Saturday week at Murrayfield, Scotland will face the All Blacks for the 34th time, the overall picture skewed ever-so-slightly in New Zealand's favour. They've won 31 and the Scots have won zero.

Draws in 1964 and 1983 - halcyon days, kind of - is as good as it has got for the underdogs since these nations first met 111 years ago.

Speaking on the BBC's Scotland Rugby Podcast on the day he announced his squad for the Nations Championship, Gregor Townsend goes through his own story with the Kiwis, about the dog days he experienced as a player - two of them ending 62-31 and 69-20 - and how the inferiority complex his generation might have felt is not the same anymore.

"It's almost like two different lifetimes," he says. "As a player, I don't think we ever felt we could win the game.

"There were moments within games over in Auckland in 1996 when we had opportunities, but they were always going to pull away from us. I've not felt that as a coach."

As coach, he has gone up against the All Blacks three times, all in Edinburgh. A 25-17 defeat in 2025, a 31-23 loss in 2023 and a 22-17 reverse in 2017.

"I felt every time we've played against them, we've had opportunities to win and the belief has been there," he said.

"We might have lacked the composure. Certainly last time, a year ago (Scotland fell 17-0 behind but then came roaring back to level at 17-17). We were just playing so much accurate, physical rugby. But we didn't take the chances.

"So there is a difference. I feel it in the players. But I didn't feel that in the 90s when we went up against them."

The coming months are seismic for Scotland with the culmination of the Nations Championship, then Townsend's final Six Nations, a World Cup warm-up against New Zealand in Dunedin, followed by the coach's last act, the World Cup itself.

Scotland have not played an away Test against the All Blacks since 2000, a two-Test deal, one in Auckland and the other at Carisbrook in Dunedin. New Zealand won the first 62-31 and the second 48-14. Townsend played in both.

Regular summer games against higher calibre southern hemisphere opposition has been crucial in Ireland's improvement in recent years, but Scotland have been denied that exposure. The global calendar has now changed and the Scots will be one of the main beneficiaries.

In Townsend's time as coach, he has had one game against the Wallabies in Australia, one against the Springboks in South Africa and none against the All Blacks in New Zealand. In the same period of time, Wales have played seven away Tests against the big three from the south, England have played nine and Ireland have had 10. Ireland have had four Tests in New Zealand in just nine years compared to Scotland's zero in 26 years.

"That's great for Scottish Rugby, great for our players to get that opportunity to play New Zealand in New Zealand," he said. "It's a really good preparation for us for the World Cup as a stand-alone game. It's one we've missed for so many years."

First Scotland call-up for Newcastle's Leatherbarrow

Townsend on Leatherbarrow call-up, Bradbury omission & World Cup hopes

Bradbury & Douglas snubbed amid left-field pick

Just when we thought the famous Toony Tombola - the expression given to Townsend's capacity for naming left-field players in his squads - had been decommissioned, he has come up with Ollie Leatherbarrow.

The 24-year-old Newcastle Red Bulls flanker has started just one game for his club this season, but he's in and Magnus Bradbury and Freddy Douglas are not. It was a surprise. To most people, at least.

"It's not a surprise for us as coaches because we've been watching him pretty regularly over the last six months," Townsend says of his new back-row. "We feel that he can cover the three positions.

"He carries really well and, when we looked at the stats for this season, the best carrying forwards that we could select, he was up there. Him and Seb Stephen [Glasgow Warriors hooker]."

Leatherbarrow, a former Scotland Under-20 player, has not started many league games - fewer than 30 - for Newcastle, or for his previous club, Exeter Chiefs. It's a huge call for the coach, who says he wants a close look at the player just to see if he's good enough to be involved beyond the autumn.

Bradbury and Douglas have been a key part in Edinburgh's march to the top of the United Rugby Championship table, so their exclusion was the big talking point.

"We feel right now is an opportunity to look at Ollie, either in that role as eight or seven, or covering all three off the bench," Townsend adds. "We have Matt Ferguson who covers eight, Josh Bayliss can play eight and both those guys have gone really well for us.

"Gregor Brown played eight against Fiji. For the Six Nations, Magnus will be one of those players in the mix. They're close decisions.

"With Freddy, there's a bit of bad luck in who he's competing against - Rory Darge, who has been our vice-captain, been our captain. He's clearly our number one openside.

"And you've got Jamie Ritchie, who covers six and seven. Josh can cover all three positions. Liam [McConnell] can cover seven, too.

"Freddy is playing really well. He's worked on parts of his game, his ball-carrying, his tackle, his dominance in tackle, and his tackle decision, whether to go for the ball or not. And he's still been able to produce those big turnovers. So, yeah, it's a good position to be in."

Scotland enlist AFL help with aerial game

Townsend has earned a reputation for innovation in the way he seeks new ideas from different sports. In this camp and for the next few weeks, Scotland have a specialist coach helping them.

Here, the name Justin Longmuir might not mean a whole lot. In Australia, he's a very big deal.

Longmuir is coach of Fremantle Dockers in the Australian Football League. He took his team all the way to the Grand Final at the end of September, where they lost agonisingly to the Brisbane Lions. Longmuir was named coach of the year regardless.

"We were speaking to Fremantle Dockers and it looked like we were getting an assistant coach to work with us," Townsend says.

"I think Kyle Steyn had mentioned it to Pete Horne [Scotland assistant coach] about trying to get someone from the AFL to help us with contesting the high ball.

"So we were excited that we were getting an assistant coach and then the head coach, Justin, said, 'I'd love to do that'.

"I'm sure our players will get tips and principles that not only they can apply over the next two weeks but they can work on and continue for the next 12 months. Already we've changed some of the language. We're using AFL language. He talks about things that we hadn't even considered - the technique of not only going up for the ball but trying to win the ball on the ground.

"When we kick now, it's about winning the ball. You win that battle, you're a long way to winning the game."

Every one of these games has enormous significance. New Zealand, Australia, Japan in the Nations Championship in November. Italy and Wales at home, France away, Ireland home and England away in the Six Nations. France home and away and then New Zealand in Dunedin as World Cup warm-ups - and then on to the biggest stage they go.

As Townsend says, this time next year Scotland will be playing knockout rugby at the World Cup. Every decision he makes from here on in will be pored over. The countdown to Australia has now started.

articles.title: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso: England winger set to return after hamstring issue
articles.summary: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso should be fit to play for England in next month's Nations Championship matches.
articles.body:
Immanuel Feyi-Waboso should be fit to play for England in next month's Nations Championship matches.

The 23-year-old limped off in the second half of Exeter's win over Newcastle earlier this month and has missed their past two matches.

But after scans over the weekend he has returned to training and could feature for Exeter in Saturday's Prem game with Harlequins.

Feyi-Waboso missed this year's Six Nations after injuring his hamstring in January but was a key part of all three of England's Nations Championship games over the summer and crossed for tries against Fiji and Argentina.

"He's an international quality player, it'd be fantastic to have him available, so let's cross fingers and hope that things keep progressing at the rate they are," Baxter told BBC Sport.

Exeter examine extent of Feyi-Waboso injury

Baxter has also been boosted by the news that the shoulder injury sustained by Australia forward Tom Hooper in Saturday's defeat at Bristol is not serious.

Hooper came off shortly before half-time against the Bears having fractured his scapula over the summer.

But the 25-year-old could be available for the Harlequins match and will be fit to play for the Wallabies next month - Australia will play England, Scotland and Wales in the Nations Championship.

"I think our prognosis at this stage is that it's been a bang, a hard bang on that fracture site that has created a pain and a numbness and a lack of mobility for hopefully for a restricted period and that we can assess him day by day now," said Baxter.

"But the one thing that's really important is there's been no catastrophic injury there, so we'll monitor him day by day and we'll see what we can get to by the end of the week."

articles.title: Nations Championship: Ireland's Garry Ringrose set to miss November Tests with hamstring injury
articles.summary: Centre Garry Ringrose is set to miss Ireland's Nations Championship fixtures next month with a hamstring injury.
articles.body:
Centre Garry Ringrose is set to miss Ireland's Nations Championship fixtures next month with a hamstring injury.

The Irish Rugby Football Union (IRFU) said on Tuesday it is "unlikely" the 31-year-old will be involved in the home matches against Argentina, Fiji and South Africa and he has remained with Leinster to continue his rehabilitation.

Ringrose, who has scored 15 tries in 76 caps, missed last weekend's United Rugby Championship win over rivals Munster at Aviva Stadium.

Fly-half Sam Prendergast remains a doubt for next week's opener with the Pumas in Dublin because of a wrist injury.

The 23-year-old is continuing his recovery with the Ireland squad after missing the Munster game, while Leinster winger Jimmy O'Brien, 29, is following return-to-play protocols after sustaining a concussion against Munster.

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell has decided against calling up any replacements despite uncertainty over Tadhg Furlong's availability.

The Leinster prop, 33, will appear before a disciplinary committee after being cited for an alleged groin grab against Munster.

Ireland beat Australia and Japan before losing to New Zealand in the southern hemisphere leg of the Nations Championship in July.

After facing Argentina on 6 November, Farrell's side host Fiji and back-to-back world champions South Africa on 14 and 21 November respectively, before a finals weekend fixture at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium on 28 and 29 November.

Argentina head coach Felipe Contepomi is faced with his own injury troubles.

Experienced Lyon prop Thomas Gallo has withdrawn from the squad with a wrist injury he sustained against Bayonne last weekend, while utility back Santiago Carreras limped off during Bath's Prem defeat by Gloucester on Friday.

"He's got to go for a scan, I'd be amazed if that's not really bad news, which is gutting for him," Bath head of rugby Johann van Graan said when asked about Carreras.

articles.title: 2026 Rugby League World Cup: England in 'do or die' game with Samoa
articles.summary: England's final group game of the 2026 women's Rugby League World Cup is "do or die", according to coach Stuart Barrow.
articles.body:
England's final group game of the 2026 women's Rugby League World Cup is "do or die", according to coach Stuart Barrow.

Barrow's side must beat Samoa in Wollongong on Friday (06.45 GMT) in order to finish second in Group A and qualify for the semi-finals.

They beat Wales 70-6 in their opener but were thrashed 78-0 by reigning champions Australia in Perth last weekend.

A win would earn England a semi-final spot, where they would most likely face New Zealand, who beat them in the last four of the previous World Cup in 2022.

"We knew we needed four points to reach the semis, and two points would likely have to come from here," Barrow told a media conference on Tuesday. "It is do or die and no-one wants to go home."

After two blow-out results, it is expected that England's final group match will be more evenly matched.

This women's World Cup has produced several mismatched results, with all the heavy defeats suffered by northern hemisphere nations inflicted by those from the south other than England beating Wales.

As well as Australia thumping England, Samoa beat Wales 76-0 and New Zealand defeated France 92-0.

It shows how much the balance of power in global rugby league lies in the southern hemisphere and Samoa's squad consists entirely of players from Australia's semi-pro NRLW, which is of a much higher standard than England's amateur Women's Super League.

Barrow says his side will have learned a lot from their hammering at the hands of co-hosts Australia in Perth last Saturday - which the NRLW described as an "annihilation" in a post on X. , external

"We have a really young group, who will be better for this experience," he said. "They now know what the game looks like against the best in the world. It was humbling, but the response has been positive.

"The speed of the ball for Australia caught our girls out. The players were saying they have never played in a game so fast in their life. We have had to look at connectivity in our defence.

"It will be a different challenge on Friday. Against Australia our attitude was really good, we were still scrambling to prevent tries in the 69th minute when 70-0 down."

Barrow has had to make changes to his squad following the loss of key player Eva Hunter to a leg injury suffered against Australia.

It has prompted a pack reshuffle, with Hollie-Mae Dodd moving from prop to the back row. Mary Coleman comes in at prop as a result.

"Eve had a scan and we are waiting on the results, but she is definitely out on Friday," Barrow said.

"She's still in her moon boot, but she is surrounded by good people and is relaxed."

England however have been boosted by captain Jodie Cunningham overcoming a nasty ear injury suffered last week and being able to be named on the bench.

Cunningham had to be rushed to hospital straight after the game for stitches to her ear, with the gory damage shared by the skipper via her Instagram page , external .

"Jodie's ear is reattached," Barrow said. "It was not pretty; you would not want your tea straight after seeing it.

"But she taped it up, got on with it [the match against Australia], then straight after the game they went straight to hospital, where they did a great job."

articles.title: Macs Page: Scarlets wing called up by Wales after Rio Dyer injury blow
articles.summary: Wales release Rio Dyer from their Nations Championship squad after hamstring injury, with Scarlets wing Macs Page added for November's games.
articles.body:
Dragons wing Rio Dyer has been released from the Wales squad for the Nations Championship because of a hamstring injury, with uncapped Scarlets back Mac Page called up.

Dyer was recalled by head coach Steve Tandy after a strong start to the season, but suffered an injury in the process of scoring against Ospreys last weekend.

The 26-year-old faces a spell on the sidelines and has been released to rehabilitate with the Rodney Parade club.

Dyer won the most recent of his 24 caps against South Africa last autumn and missed out on the Six Nations and summer squads.

His misfortune opens the door for uncapped Page, who is called up despite a head injury suffered for Scarlets at Stormers last Saturday.

Scarlets back in-form Page to earn Wales Test call

Lewis conquers self-doubt to hunt more Wales caps

Page scored his fifth try of the season in Cape Town but then hit his head heavily on the ground when attempting to get his sixth.

The 21-year-old was given oxygen as he was helped from the field and will go through the return-to-play protocols before pushing for a first cap.

He joins Scarlets team-mates Ellis Mee and Blair Murray as an option in the back three along with Louis Rees-Zammit, Tom Rogers, Josh Adams and Gabriel Hamer-Webb.

Page, who can also play at outside centre, was a member of Wales' touring party to Japan in 2025 but did not feature.

Wales play Japan in Cardiff on Saturday, 7 November and then host New Zealand and Australia.

Tandy's side then take on another southern hemisphere opponent on Nations Championship finals weekend at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium at the end of the month.

articles.title: Steve Borthwick lays down World Cup challenge to England with 10 Tests left before squad selection
articles.summary: England have 12 Tests until the Rugby World Cup which takes place in Australia in 2027; Steve Borthwick believes he is nearing a decision on which players will make his final squad; England take on Australia, Japan, and New Zealand in Autumn Nations Series
articles.body:
England have an upcoming three-day training camp ahead of the Autumn Nations Series for which Borthwick has named a 36-player squad which will gather at England's performance centre at Pennyhill Park.

England will face Australia, Japan and New Zealand throughout November, in a series that represents their final opportunity to test themselves against southern hemisphere opposition before the Rugby World Cup.

It means Borthwick is already keeping a close eye on his players, knowing that he will soon be approaching the selection of his 33-man squad to travel down under and face Tonga, Zimbabwe and Wales in the World Cup pool stage.

Although the challenge is considerable, Borthwick is eager to see how his side perform as players seize their opportunities to prove they deserve to represent England on rugby's biggest stage.

"It is a hugely exciting period. I think this team is an exciting team. It's got so much talent and so many young players coming through with so much ability," Borthwick told Sky Sports .

"As I framed it to the players, we've got 12 Tests now to the World Cup. We have got 10 Tests until I name a 33-man squad that goes to the World Cup.

"I said, effectively, I am not going to bring in a large training squad, I am going to bring in a squad that has everybody in contention for selection for that 33.

"This is the last chance we will have the team playing against the southern hemisphere opposition before we get to that World Cup.

"I am really looking forward to seeing how the players face against this calibre opponent, this type of opponent, the way they play, coming off the schedule they come off, where they've been in camp for a long period of time and played a number of Test matches.

Is Borthwick close to knowing his best team?

So, just how close is Borthwick to settling on his strongest side? Perhaps closer than many might expect, with the England head coach making it "clear" that more than 20 players are already firmly in contention for selection. He will continue to back those players as they look to cement their places in the squad.

"I think it is a very consistent feeling. I think out of the 33-man Rugby World Cup squad, I'd be very confident that somewhere in the mid-to-high 20s of players, I think they'll be at the World Cup," added Borthwick.

"I have been very clear to the players about that. If you look at my selections, you will see there's been a lot of consistency of selection and backing the players.

"So, not chopping and changing them from one game to the next, but backing the players to go and perform.

"As with every World Cup squad I've selected, a huge amount of time is spent debating the final few places. Positional versatility and flexibility are invaluable, as are players who are ready to step up and bring the right character to the squad."

In September, reports emerged that Borthwick was set to have his contract extended beyond the 2028 Six Nations in a move designed to avoid uncertainty over his future ahead of and during next year's Rugby World Cup.

The England head coach has retained the backing of the Rugby Football Union (RFU) despite a "challenging" review of the Six Nations campaign, in which England suffered four defeats in five matches.

Although speculation surrounding his future has intensified in recent months, Borthwick insists he has always understood the pressure that comes with leading England and is prepared to embrace the responsibility.

"I think that for us, the focus has been very much upon the World Cup and this challenge you have in this role," he said.

"Where you focus on the World Cup, which is now a year away, and the game that's immediately in front of you. I don't think my focus has ever changed. I don't think my assistant coach's focus has ever changed.

"With the amount of preparation time we have, we need to maximise every minute. So I don't think it really comes into a factor within consideration.

"When you coach in England, the expectation of the millions of people that watch it, it is wonderful.

"Lots of people say they want to go and coach and actually the reality is very different. I love this role, I love coaching this team, and I am fortunate to have a fantastic group of coaches to work with and a brilliant group of players that are keen to learn and continue their development journey."

articles.title: Steve Borthwick: England preparation time for Nations Championship opener 'a challenge'
articles.summary: England head coach Steve Borthwick says his players have tried to make most of limited preparation time for their Test against a comparatively battle-hardened Australia.
articles.body:
England coach Steve Borthwick says his players have tried to make most of limited preparation time for their Test against a comparatively battle-hardened Australia.

Borthwick has just finished working with his squad during a three-day training camp before they return to their club sides on Wednesday.

England face Australia in their opening match of this autumn's Nations Championship campaign at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on Sunday, 8 November.

While England must balance their international preparations with the demands of the Premiership season, the Wallabies have much more time to focus on forthcoming matches.

Australia have played 10 Tests since July, including matches against South Africa and New Zealand.

"It's a case of doing more of less," Borthwick told BBC rugby union correspondent Chris Jones.

"Identifying the clear priorities and chasing them and not being side-tracked, not deviating from that.

"I think this is one of the challenges, particularly balancing the different stakeholders [the clubs and the national set-up]."

England's preparations have also been affected by the Prem schedule, with players involved in Sunday's fixtures having less time for full squad training.

"We had a session today really that was affected obviously by the fact that we had a Sunday game in Prem Rugby," Borthwick explained.

"Fortunately, we don't have any Sunday games this coming week in Prem Rugby, which I'm pleased about.

"So that should allow players to be recovered in a proper run into the Test match."

Borthwick acknowledged the challenge of balancing club and international commitments, but said playing at the weekend could benefit England.

"They'll go back and play the rugby and in so many ways that will be a positive for us for next weekend," he said.

"The players are match fit at club level, playing regularly at club level, and as long as they don't get injured, then they're all available for selection next week, then that will be positive.

"I'd say on one side, I think it's a real strength of English rugby that the players have such great loyalty and passion for their clubs as we saw very evidently in this last round with the derbies that went on.

"They are team-mates and best of mates the next day for a couple of days [with England] and then they go back to being rivals again until they come back into camp next week."

Borthwick also identified the breakdown as an area where England need to adapt to the demands of international rugby.

He pointed to the recent European fixtures, in which English clubs collectively lost more of their own breakdown ball and won less opposition breakdown ball than teams from other competing nations.

"Part of my job is identify those bits of where I need to bridge from where the players are in Prem rugby to where they are in Test rugby," he said.

"The level of competition [at the breakdown] is at a different level in Test rugby."
